purpose: Clozapine is used to treat severe schizophrenia, especially when other medications have not worked well enough. It can also help reduce the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in people with schizophrenia or a related condition called schizoaffective disorder. It is usually tried after at least two other antipsychotic medicines have been given a fair chance and did not help enough.
how_it_works: Clozapine works by balancing certain chemical messengers in your brain, mainly dopamine and serotonin, which can become imbalanced in schizophrenia. By calming overactive signals in the brain, it helps reduce symptoms like hallucinations, confused thinking, and feeling disconnected from reality. Think of it like a volume control that turns down the 'noise' in your brain that is causing distress.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling very sleepy, drooling especially at night, dizziness when standing up, weight gain, constipation, fast heartbeat, blurry vision, increased sweating, and dry mouth are all commonly reported. Most of these tend to improve over time as your body adjusts to the medication.
warnings: The most serious risk is a dangerous drop in white blood cells called agranulocytosis, which can make it very hard for your body to fight infections — this is why you MUST get regular blood tests while taking this medicine. It can also cause seizures, especially at higher doses, and a rare but serious heart condition called myocarditis. Because of these risks, clozapine is only available through a special safety program, and your pharmacist and doctor will monitor you closely. Tell your doctor right away if you develop fever, sore throat, flu-like symptoms, chest pain, or fast or irregular heartbeat.
typical_dosing: Clozapine is usually started at a very low dose, often 12.5 mg to 25 mg once or twice a day, and then slowly increased over weeks to find the right dose for you. Most people end up taking between 300 mg and 450 mg per day, split into two or three doses, though some people need higher amounts. Your doctor will adjust your dose carefully based on how you respond and how well you tolerate it — never change your dose on your own.
